title: Lonicera maackii

{{Short description|Species of plant in the family Caprifoliaceae native to eastern Asia}} {{use dmy dates|date=September 2020}} {{speciesbox |image = Lonicera_maackii_2.jpg |genus = Lonicera |species = maackii |authority = ([[Franz Josef Ruprecht|Rupr.]]) [[Carl Maximowicz|Maxim.]] |synonyms = {{Plainlist | style = margin-left: 1em; text-indent: -1em; | *''Xylosteon maackii'' Rupr. }} |synonyms_ref = {{cite web |title=The Plant List: A working list of all plant species |url=http://www.theplantlist.org/tpl1.1/record/tro-6000471 |access-date=7 December 2014}} |}} '''''Lonicera maackii''''', the '''Amur honeysuckle''', is a species of [[honeysuckle]] in the family [[Caprifoliaceae]] that is native to temperate eastern [[Asia]]; specifically in northern and western [[China]] south to [[Yunnan]], [[Mongolia]], [[Primorsky Krai]] in southeastern [[Siberia]], [[Korea]], and, albeit rare there, central and northern [[Honshū]], [[Japan]].{{GRIN |access-date=2 January 2018}} ''Lonicera maackii'' is a listed [[endangered species]] in [[Japan]].{{cite web |title=Red List of Threatened Plants of Japan |type=Excel spreadsheet |department=Ministry of the Environment |publisher=Government of Japan |language=en |url=http://www.biodic.go.jp/english/rdb/red_plants.csv}}{{cite book |article=''Lonicera maackii'' (with map) |title=Red Data Book (Japan) |language=ja |url=http://www.rdbplants.jp/RDB/map/sp-5/2/5281.htm |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110615092327/http://www.rdbplants.jp/RDB/map/sp-5/2/5281.htm |archive-date=2011-06-15 |postscript=;}} {{cite web |title=Google translation |language=en |url=https://translate.google.com/translate?hl=en&sl=ja&u=http://www.rdbplants.jp/RDB/map/sp-5/2/5281.htm&sa=X&oi=translate&resnum=10&}} It has [[escaped plant|escaped from cultivation]] and [[Naturalisation (biology)|naturalized]] in [[New Zealand]] and the eastern [[United States]]; in the [[woodland]]s of the U.S. it is a significant [[invasive species]]. ==Description== [[File:Amur honeysuckle (Lonicera maackii).jpg|thumb|close up on the plant]] The plant is a large, [[deciduous]] [[shrub]] that grows a maximum of {{convert|6|m|ft|0}} tall with stems of a maximum of {{convert|10|cm|in|0}} in diameter. The [[leaf|leaves]] are oppositely arranged, {{convert|5–9|cm|in|frac=2}} long and {{convert|2–4|cm|in|frac=8}} broad, with an entire margin, and with at least some rough [[Pubescent (botany)|pubescence]]. [[File:LoniceraMaackii5.jpg|left|thumb|Foliage and fruit]] The [[flower]]s are produced in pairs; they are {{convert|2|cm|in|frac=8}} long, have two lips, begin white and later turn yellow or pale orange in color; they bloom from middle of spring to early summer. The [[fruit]] is a bright red to black, semi-translucent [[berry (botany)|berry]], {{convert|2–6|mm|in|frac=128}} in diameter, that contains numerous small [[seed]]s. ===Etymology and authority=== [[File:LoniceraMackii4.jpg|right|thumb|''Lonicera maackii'' planted as a hedge]] The species name "''maackii''" is derived from [[Richard Maack]], a [[Russia]]n naturalist of the 19th century. Its common name "Amur honeysuckle" is from its native range surrounding the [[Amur River]], which demarcates the border between [[Siberia]] and [[Manchuria]]. :Some [[Internet]] sources name the species authority as "(Rupr.) Herder", but the correct authority is "(Rupr.) Maxim". ===Cultivation=== Amur honeysuckle is cultivated as an [[ornamental plant]] for its attractive flowers and as a [[hedge (barrier)|hedge]]. Many [[cultivar]]s have been selected for [[horticulture]], including "Erubescens" with pink flowers and "Rem Red" with an erect form. The plant is adaptable and flourishes in a wide range of conditions. In the United States, it was planted to control erosion and to form hedges. It readily self-propagates via birds [[seed dispersal|dispersing]] its seeds, and quickly spreads into habitats for which it has no community connectivity. It grows rapidly and prefers shady habitats such as [[woodland]] [[understory|understories]], neglected [[urban area]]s, and [[fence]] rows. It can form very dense thickets.{{cite book |editor-last=Huxley |editor-first=A. |year=1992 |title=New RHS Dictionary of Gardening |publisher=Macmillan |isbn=0-333-47494-5}}{{cite web |title=''Lonicera maackii'' in Missouri |website=Missouriplants |url=http://www.missouriplants.com/Whiteopp/Lonicera_maackii_page.html}}{{cite web |title=''Lonicera'' species |series=Invasive weeds from Asia |website=Invasive.org |url=http://www.invasive.org/weeds/asian/lonicera.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060928013712/http://www.invasive.org/weeds/asian/lonicera.pdf |archive-date=2006-09-28}} The flowers are sometimes savored by [[child]]ren, who remove blossoms and pull off their bottoms so as to suck out the sweet [[nectar]] in the centers. The berries, on the other hand, are mildly [[poison]]ous to humans and therefore should not be consumed. ===Alternatives=== Because of the invasive nature of this species, regardless of whether it is banned locally, it is imprudent to cultivate Amur honeysuckle in climates similar to those where the species has invaded, e.g. eastern [[North America]]. Possible alternative shrubs that are also fast growing, shade tolerant, and deciduous, but not invasive in eastern US include: {{col-begin}} {{col-break|width=5%}} {{col-break|width=30%}} ''[[Calycanthus floridus]]''
''[[Cornus sericea]]''
''[[Hydrangea]]'' species
{{col-break|width=30%}} ''[[Viburnum cassinoides]]''
''[[Viburnum dentatum]]''
{{col-break|width=30%}} ''[[Viburnum prunifolium]]''
''[[Viburnum trilobum]]''
{{col-end}} More native shrubs for use the Midwestern United States are listed in the pamphlet ''Curse of the Bush Honeysuckles!''.{{cite web |title=Curse of the Bush Honeysuckles! |website=mdc.mo.gov |publisher=Missouri Department of Conservation |url=https://mdc.mo.gov/sites/default/files/downloads/CurseBushHoneysuckle.pdf}} == Phytochemistry == ''L. maackii'' produces various [[secondary metabolites]] to deter [[insect herbivory]].{{Cite journal |url=https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/pdf/10.1086/526470 |title= Contrasting Effects of Allelochemicals from Two Invasive Plants on the Performance of a Nonmycorrhizal Plant |last=Cipollini |journal= International Journal of Plant Sciences |display-authors=et al. |date=March–April 2008 |volume= 169 |issue= 3 |pages= 371–375 |doi=10.1086/526470|bibcode= 2008IJPlS.169..371C |url-access=subscription }} Cipollini et al. found seasonal variation in the levels of [[chlorogenic acid]], [[apigenin]], [[apigenin-7-glucoside]], [[luteolin]] and [[luteolin-7-glucoside]], and confirm their deterrent effect.{{cite journal | last1=Peñuelas | first1=Josep | last2=Sardans | first2=Jordi | last3=Estiarte | first3=Marc | last4=Ogaya | first4=Romà | last5=Carnicer | first5=Jofre | last6=Coll | first6=Marta | last7=Barbeta | first7=Adria | last8=Rivas-Ubach | first8=Albert | last9=Llusià | first9=Joan | last10=Garbulsky | first10=Martin | last11=Filella | first11=Iolanda | last12=Jump | first12=Alistair S. | title=Evidence of current impact of climate change on life: a walk from genes to the biosphere | journal=[[Global Change Biology]] | publisher=[[Wiley Publishing|Wiley]] | volume=19 | issue=8 | date=2013-03-25 | issn=1354-1013 | doi=10.1111/gcb.12143 | pages=2303–2338 | pmid=23505157 | bibcode=2013GCBio..19.2303P | citeseerx=10.1.1.480.9111| s2cid=10377923 }} == Invasive nature and remedies == Birds and mammals consume and disperse seeds. Biotic transmission vectors include species: [[American robin]] (''Turdus migratorius''), [[hermit thrush]] (''Catharus guttatus'') and [[European starling]] (''Sturnus vulgaris'') and [[white-tailed deer]] (''Odocoileus virginianus'').{{Cite report |title=Lonicera maackii (Amur honeysuckle) |last=Kaufman |first=S |date=2022-01-07 |doi=10.1079/cabicompendium.31192 |language=en|doi-access=free }} Because of its well-documented invasiveness, propagation of this plant is illegal or controlled in some of the United States, where it is an alien species.{{cite web |title=Amur honeysuckle |series=Weed of the Week Fact Sheet |department=USDA Forest Service |publisher=United States Department of Agriculture (USDA) |url=http://www.na.fs.fed.us/fhp/invasive_plants/weeds/amur-honeysuckle.pdf}}{{cite web |title=Annotated bibliography of primary research on invasive qualities of ''L. maackii'' in the U.S.A. |series=National Biological Information Infrastructure |publisher=University of Tennessee |place=Knoxville, TN |url=http://sain.utk.edu/invasives/species44.shtml |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://archive.today/20070513173958/http://sain.utk.edu/invasives/species44.shtml |archive-date=2007-05-13 }}{{cite web |title=''L. maackii'' |series=Plant Database |department=Department of Horticulture |publisher=University of Connecticut |url=http://www.hort.uconn.edu/Plants/l/lonmaa/lonmaa1.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070510024414/http://www.hort.uconn.edu/Plants/l/lonmaa/lonmaa1.html |archive-date=2007-05-10}}{{cite web |publisher=Ohio State University |series=Pocket Gardener |title=''L. maackii'' |url=http://hcs.osu.edu/pocketgardener/source/description/lo_ackii.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070714040836/http://hcs.osu.edu/pocketgardener/source/description/lo_ackii.html |archive-date=2007-07-14}} The species is classified "invasive, banned" in [[Connecticut]], "prohibited" in [[Massachusetts]], as an invasive species in [[Tennessee]], as an invasive species in [[Ohio]], as a "Class B noxious [[weed]]" in [[Vermont]], and as an invasive species in [[Wisconsin]].{{cite web |title=''L. maackii'' |series=USDA Plants Database |publisher=United States Department of Agriculture (USDA) |url=https://plants.usda.gov/java/profile?symbol=LOMA6}} It has been suggested that plants growing outside their native range, in eastern Asia, should be removed and replaced by non-invasive alternatives. A 2016 review paper details the variety of competitive advantages this subcanopy woody species has over native plants in eastern North America and confirms that even the most successful combinations of stem cutting followed by herbicide application are not capable of killing all the individuals. The conclusion is that once this species has established, management interventions will need to continue into the future.{{cite journal |last1=McNeish |first1=Rachel E |last2=McEwan |first2=Ryan W |title=A review on the invasion ecology of Amur honeysuckle (Lonicera maackii, Caprifoliaceae) a case study of ecological impacts at multiple scales |journal=Torrey Botanical Society |date=2016 |volume=143 |issue=4 |pages=367–385 |doi=10.3159/TORREY-D-15-00049.1 |bibcode=2016JTBS..143..367M |url=https://www.strategian.com/fulltext/McNeish2016a.pdf}}{{Cite journal |last=McNeish |first=Rachel E. |last2=Benbow |first2=M. Eric |last3=McEwan |first3=Ryan W. |date=September 2017 |title=Removal of the Invasive Shrub, Lonicera maackii (Amur Honeysuckle), from a Headwater Stream Riparian Zone Shifts Taxonomic and Functional Composition of the Aquatic Biota |url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/invasive-plant-science-and-management/article/removal-of-the-invasive-shrub-lonicera-maackii-amur-honeysuckle-from-a-headwater-stream-riparian-zone-shifts-taxonomic-and-functional-composition-of-the-aquatic-biota/FF381E0CB1D2B4FE82A7D8F26DFE4010 |journal=Invasive Plant Science and Management |language=en |volume=10 |issue=3 |pages=232–246 |doi=10.1017/inp.2017.22 |issn=1939-7291}} ===Consequences=== [[File:Lonicera maackii along Huron River of Michigan 02.jpg|thumb|''Lonicera maacki'' dominates the subcanopy along this stretch of the Huron River near Ypsilanti, Michigan.|right|upright=1.75]] In the understories of deciduous woodlands of the eastern United States it forms dense thickets, the shade of whose canopies prevent the growth of native shrubs, juvenile trees, and wild flowers. Uncontrolled, these growths result in almost [[monoculture|monocultural]] thickets of Amur honeysuckle. The species gravely jeopardizes not only the diversity of the invaded ecosystems but even the regeneration of woodlands, because it reduces the growth and diversity of native seedlings.{{cite journal |first1=David L. |last1=Gorchov |first2=Donald E. |last2=Trisel |date=1 May 2003 |title=Competitive effects of the invasive shrub, Lonicera maackii (Rupr.) Herder (Caprifoliaceae), on the growth and survival of native tree seedlings |journal=Plant Ecology |volume=166 |issue=1 |pages=13–24 |doi=10.1023/A:1023208215796|bibcode=2003PlEco.166...13G |s2cid=41965189 }} Additional studies indicate that it negatively affects birds{{cite journal |first1=Kenneth A. |last1=Schmidt |first2=Christopher J. |last2=Whelan |date=1 December 1999 |title=Effects of Exotic Lonicera and Rhamnus on Songbird Nest Predation |journal=Conservation Biology |volume=13 |issue=6 |pages=1502–1506 |doi=10.1046/j.1523-1739.1999.99050.x|bibcode=1999ConBi..13.1502S |s2cid=85797805 }} and tadpoles.{{cite journal |first1=J.I. |last1=Watling |first2=C.R. |last2=Hickman |first3=E. |last3=Lee |first4=K. |last4=Wang |first5=J.L. |last5=Orrock |date=1 January 2011 |title=Extracts of the invasive shrub Lonicera maackii increase mortality and alter behavior of amphibian larvae |journal=Oecologia |volume=165 |issue=1 |pages=153–159 |doi=10.1007/s00442-010-1777-z |pmid=20938785|bibcode=2011Oecol.165..153W |s2cid=7347009 }} However, other studies have shown a mixture of positive and negative effects on birds, depending on species (McNeish and McEwan, 2016).{{Cite journal|doi=10.3159/TORREY-D-15-00049.1|title=A review on the invasion ecology of Amur honeysuckle (Lonicera maackii, Caprifoliaceae) a case study of ecological impacts at multiple scales|year=2016|last1=McNeish|first1=Rachel E.|last2=McEwan|first2=Ryan W.|journal=The Journal of the Torrey Botanical Society|volume=143|issue=4|pages=367–385|s2cid=89223917|doi-access=free |bibcode=2016JTBS..143..367M }} Effects on invertebrate diversity can also be negative or positive, depending on the taxonomic group (Loomis and Cameron, 2014).{{Cite journal|url=https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10530-013-0505-0|doi = 10.1007/s10530-013-0505-0|title = Impact of the invasive shrub Amur honeysuckle (Lonicera maackii) on shrub-layer insects in a deciduous forest in the eastern United States|year = 2014|last1 = Loomis|first1 = Jessica D.|last2 = Cameron|first2 = Guy N.|journal = Biological Invasions|volume = 16| issue=1 |pages = 89–100| bibcode=2014BiInv..16...89L |s2cid = 18834906|url-access = subscription}} Even if ''L. maackii'' shrubs are removed, the affected habitat may not recover absent substantial restoration effort.{{cite journal |last1=Rodewald |first1=A.D. |display-authors=etal |year=2015 |title=Does removal of invasives restore ecological networks? An experimental approach |journal=Biological Invasions |volume=17 |issue=7 |pages=2139–2146 |doi=10.1007/s10530-015-0866-7 |bibcode=2015BiInv..17.2139R |s2cid=14654835 |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/273898322|hdl=10261/116766 |hdl-access=free }} The relationship between white-tailed deer and ''L. maackii'' is complex, with deer playing a significant role in consuming the berries, dispersing the seeds, and browsing the foliage; the presence of ''L. maackii'' may prevent deer from browsing understory vegetation, which can be desirable if a native understory is present, but undesirable if other invasive species dominate the understory. A study conducted in the vicinity of St. Louis, Missouri in 2010 indicated that the plant increases the risk of [[tick]]-borne diseases such as [[Erlichiosis]] and [[Lyme disease]] in suburban natural areas by attracting [[deer]] and consequently increasing the presence of infected ticks. Furthermore, experimental removal of the plant was shown to reduce [[deer]] activity and the number of infected [[ticks]] by shifting ticks' blood meals from deer.{{cite journal |first1=Brian F. |last1=Allan |first2=Humberto P. |last2=Dutra |first3=Lisa S. |last3=Goessling |first4=Kirk |last4=Barnett |first5=Jonathan M. |last5=Chase |first6=Robert J. |last6=Marquis |first7=Genevieve |last7=Pang |first8=Gregory A. |last8=Storch |first9=Robert E. |last9=Thach |first10=John L. |last10=Orrock |display-authors=6 |date=26 October 2010 |title=Invasive honeysuckle eradication reduces tick-borne disease risk by altering host dynamics |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |volume=107 |issue=43 |pages=18523–18527 |doi=10.1073/pnas.1008362107 |pmid=20937859 |pmc=2973004 |doi-access=free |bibcode=2010PNAS..10718523A }} ===Control and eradication=== The species is controlled by cutting, flaming, or burning the plant to the level of its roots and repetition of this in two-week increments until the nutrient reserves in the roots are depleted and unable to produce any new growths. To ensure eradication, [[herbicide]] may be applied to freshly cut stumps. Control by [[prescribed burn]]ing has been found to be most effective during the phase of seed dispersal in late summer and early autumn. It can also be controlled by annual applications of [[glyphosate]] that thoroughly saturate the foliage, or by [[grubbing]] the shallowly rooted juvenile plants, but these two methods increase labor cost and disrupt the soil. Uprooting by hand or with tools can be effective for small plants, though it becomes difficult or impractical for larger ones.{{Cite web |title=Shrub Honeysuckles |url=https://extension.psu.edu/shrub-honeysuckles |access-date=2023-03-29 |website=extension.psu.edu |language=en}} This species has been found to be a host for the leaf-mining moth ''[[Phyllonorycter emberizaepenella]]'' in North America.{{Cite journal|last=Craves|first=J.A.|date=2017|title=Native birds exploit leaf-mining moth larvae using a new North American host, non-native Lonicera maackii|url=https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/11956860.2017.1367908?journalCode=teco20|journal=[[Écoscience]]|volume=24|issue=3–4 |pages=81–90|doi=10.1080/11956860.2017.1367908|bibcode=2017Ecosc..24...81C |s2cid=90390095|url-access=subscription}} In its native range, ''Lonicera maackii'' is a host plant for the following butterflies: ''[[Limenitis camilla]]'', ''[[Limenitis helmanni]]'', and ''Limenitis amphyssa''.{{Cite web |title=HOSTS - a Database of the World's Lepidopteran Hostplants - HOSTS - Data Portal |url=https://data.nhm.ac.uk/dataset/hosts/resource/877f387a-36a3-486c-a0c1-b8d5fb69f85a?q=lonicera+maackii&view_id=e2a17eb7-1c7c-4d41-9d95-7c697f5d50ab&field=Damage&value= |access-date=2024-06-08 |website=data.nhm.ac.uk |language=en}} == References == {{reflist|25em}} {{Commons}} {{Taxonbar|from=Q1076276}} [[Category:Lonicera|maackii]] [[Category:Flora of Northeast Asia]] [[Category:Garden plants of Asia]] [[Category:Taxa named by Karl Maximovich]]
